journal_name: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction

abstracts.abstract:
The landscape of human-computer interaction is undergoing a fundamental transformation as AI systems evolve from passive tools to active collaborators. However, existing HCI theories predominantly address human-dominated interaction paradigms, lacking comprehensive frameworks for understanding this paradigm shift. This paper introduces the Human-AI Collaborative Cognition (HACC) framework, a novel theoretical model that integrates distributed cognition theory with active inference principles to explain how humans and AI agents co-construct understanding and make decisions together. The HACC framework comprises three core dimensions: agency, participation, and emergence. We validate this theoretical contribution through three empirical studies spanning AI-assisted design, collaborative writing, and intelligent decision support scenarios. Data collection involved interviews, interaction observations, and analysis of collaborative interaction logs across 48 participants. Our findings reveal that the agency dimension illuminates mechanisms of trust calibration between humans and AI systems, while the participation dimension characterizes how task ownership and collaborative intent are dynamically negotiated. Most significantly, the emergence dimension demonstrates that collaborative cognitive capabilities can exceed the sum of individual contributions, suggesting emergent properties unique to human-AI co-cognition. This research contributes a foundational theoretical shift from viewing HCI as bilateral interaction toward understanding it as collaborative cognition, offering designers and researchers new conceptual tools for creating AI-integrated interaction systems that honor human agency while leveraging machine intelligence.

Keywords: human-AI collaboration, distributed cognition, active inference, collaborative interaction, theoretical framework

Heuristic evaluation remains one of the most widely adopted usability inspection methods for user interface design, yet its application to mobile interaction contexts has received limited systematic attention. Traditional usability heuristics were developed primarily for desktop systems and fail to adequately address the unique challenges of mobile use contexts, including fragmented interaction patterns, attention management across modalities, and context-sensitive design requirements. This paper presents an enhanced framework for mobile usability evaluation that significantly extends existing heuristic approaches. We propose twelve context-aware heuristics specifically designed for mobile HCI, derived through a rigorous card sorting study with 24 usability experts and validated through iterative refinement. The framework introduces three assessment modules: contextual inquiry, heuristic inspection, and experience sampling, enabling evaluators to capture usability issues that emerge in authentic mobile usage scenarios. We conducted a comparative evaluation with 60 participants assessing five contemporary mobile applications, comparing our enhanced framework against traditional heuristic evaluation and think-aloud protocols. Results demonstrate that our context-aware approach identified 47% more mobile-specific usability problems, including critical issues related to attention interruption, single-handed operation difficulties, and context transition failures. Additionally, the framework achieved 33% higher problem detection efficiency while maintaining acceptable precision rates. This research contributes a significantly improved evaluation methodology specifically tailored to the demands of mobile interaction design, advancing the state of usability engineering practice in the mobile HCI domain.

Keywords: usability evaluation, mobile interaction, heuristic evaluation, contextual analysis, evaluation methods

Contemporary computer-supported cooperative work systems predominantly emphasize task coordination through structured interfaces while inadequately supporting the affective and intentional dimensions of collaborative work. This limitation manifests most acutely in distributed teams, where members experience diminished awareness of colleagues' cognitive and emotional states, leading to coordination breakdowns and reduced team cohesion. This paper introduces the Affective Collaborative Space (ACS), a novel collaborative work environment that integrates multimodal emotion recognition with spatial computing to render team members' emotional states and collaborative intentions perceptible in real-time. The ACS architecture combines facial expression analysis, voice prosody interpretation, and physiological signal processing to construct a comprehensive model of team affective dynamics. This emotional awareness is then spatially represented through ambient visualization techniques, creating a shared virtual workspace where teams can perceive each other's cognitive engagement, creative momentum, and interpersonal tension. We conducted a longitudinal study with two geographically distributed software teams over eight weeks, comparing ACS-assisted collaboration against traditional video conferencing conditions. Quantitative results revealed significant improvements in team cohesion scores and 28% faster task completion times. Qualitative analysis uncovered that emotional transparency facilitated more effective turn-taking in discussions and earlier conflict resolution. User experience data demonstrated that participants developed heightened awareness of collaborative rhythms and reported feeling more connected to remote colleagues. This research introduces a paradigm-shifting approach to collaborative system design that foregrounds affective computing within CSCW, demonstrating that emotional perception fundamentally transforms the quality of distributed teamwork.

Keywords: emotion recognition, collaborative interface, spatial computing, affective computing, teamwork

Despite widespread recognition of accessibility as a fundamental design requirement, current design toolchains maintain significant gaps between accessibility principles and practical implementation. Designers frequently address accessibility as an afterthought, resulting in costly remediation efforts and exclusionary experiences for users with disabilities. This paper presents the Inclusive Design Workflow System (IDWS), a comprehensive toolkit that integrates accessibility verification directly into mainstream design processes and design systems. The IDWS architecture comprises three integrated components: an Accessibility-Aware Component Library containing pre-built accessible design patterns, a Real-time Accessibility Engine that performs continuous automated checking during the design phase, and an Intelligent Remediation Module providing contextual repair suggestions. We implemented IDWS as a Figma plugin integrated with continuous integration pipelines, enabling designers to identify and address accessibility issues during natural design workflows rather than post-hoc auditing. Evaluation involved partnership with three design organizations developing production applications, assessing both process efficiency and outcome quality. Quantitative findings indicate that the system automatically detects 87% of common accessibility violations and reduces designer remediation time by 62%. Critically, user testing with 45 participants including users with various disabilities demonstrated a 34% improvement in task completion rates for applications designed using IDWS compared to baseline conditions. Qualitative feedback revealed that designers found the integrated approach less burdensome than separate accessibility audits and appreciated receiving specific remediation guidance. This research contributes a significantly improved design methodology that makes accessibility integration feasible within contemporary agile development contexts, advancing inclusive design practice from specialized expertise to standard workflow.

Keywords: accessibility, inclusive design, design system, universal design, assistive technology
